model_output.score_comment_short: Your recent work has useful account detail, but few measured results.
model_output.score_comment_long: The current role names your account book, review audience, and team-wide onboarding checklist. It says less about renewal results or how you handle a payroll escalation. Adding those details, where you can verify them, would make the work easier to assess.
model_output.score_plain: Your resume gives a reviewer a concrete picture of your customer success work. For a role with explicit retention targets, it leaves an important comparison unanswered.
model_output.first_impression: You manage 48 mid-market accounts in payroll software and work across the customer lifecycle. The checklist used by the whole CS team is worth keeping because it shows your work extends beyond your own accounts.

model_output.summary: Your move from tier-2 payroll support into customer success connects product problems with ongoing account relationships. The current title and account book place you at the Customer Success Manager level. You work with finance and HR leads and coordinate with Sales, Support, and Product. The resume doesn't show retention or expansion results, so the fit with this job's commercial targets remains uncertain.
strengths: Your 94% customer satisfaction score across 2021 gives the support role a concrete result.
Quarterly reviews with finance and HR leads show experience working with more than one customer function.
Gainsight and Salesforce are named in your skills and also appear in the job description.
gaps: The resume doesn't state whether you have been accountable for gross retention, net retention, or expansion targets, which are central to this role.
It doesn't explain whether you use product usage data to identify risk, so your approach to early intervention is unclear.
The seniority of the finance and HR leads in your reviews isn't specified, leaving VP-level sponsor experience unconfirmed.
